title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
key_facts: Quanta Magazine interviewed Moritz Hardt, a computer scientist and director at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems.
Hardt's 2026 book is The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks; he calls benchmarks "the mistake that made machine learning".
He says the benchmarking ecosystem is broken, and that absolute scores on a benchmark do not mean much.
He says rankings of models, by contrast, have historically stayed stable across different datasets, which is why machine learning escaped a scientific crisis.
That stability needs models to train on the same data; with LLMs the training data is unknown and builders can assemble data mixes that promote benchmark performance.
He proposes "altitude training": giving every model a little benchmark-relevant preparation to level the playing field and restore the validity of rankings.
He says benchmarking can in the long run lead to new scientific knowledge, citing the CASP protein-folding benchmark.
quote_evidence: In his 2026 book The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks, Hardt makes the provocative case that these measuring sticks have been broken for decades already
Hardt cautions that the scores AI models receive on benchmarks don’t mean much. But comparisons, or rankings, among models do.
The problem is not so much that people optimize to the benchmarks — it’s that they optimize to different degrees.
why_it_matters_hint: Benchmarks decide how AI models are judged and sold; a researcher says the system is broken but fixable.
notes: A condensed and edited interview; the views are Hardt's, and the fix is a proposal.
